model.title: Economic and budgetary surveillance of Member States in the euro area experiencing or threatened with serious difficulties with respect to their financial stability

summary.lead: Official summary (Legislative Observatory, Decision by Parliament, 1st reading):

blocks.text: The European Parliament adopted by 458 votes to 138, with 61 abstentions, a legislative resolution on the proposal for a regulation of the European Parliament and of the Council amending Regulation (EU) No 472/2013 as regards the economic and budgetary surveillance of Member States in the euro area experiencing or threatened with serious difficulties with respect to their financial stability.
The European Parliament adopted its position at first reading by amending the Commission's proposal.

Parliament supports the Commission's proposal to amend the enhanced post-programme surveillance regulation for euro area Member States facing or at risk of experiencing serious financial difficulties (Regulation (EU) No 472/2013) in order to ensure consistency between that regulation and the reformed economic governance framework of the Union.

The amendments consist of eliminating inconsistencies with legislative acts resulting from the reform of the Union's economic governance framework carried out in 2024 and with institutional developments since 2013, as well as simplifying and clarifying certain elements in line with the Commission's simplification agenda, which aims to reduce regulatory burdens and simplify EU legislation to facilitate its implementation.

Where a Member State requests financial assistance from one or more other Member States or third countries, the European Financial Stability Mechanism (EFSM), the European Stability Mechanism (ESM), or the IMF, it must prepare, in agreement with the Commission, acting in liaison with the ECB and, where appropriate, the IMF, a draft macroeconomic adjustment programme that includes annual budgetary targets. In accordance with Regulation (EU) 2024/1263, where a Member State has an active national medium-term fiscal and structural plan and is subsequently subject to a macroeconomic adjustment programme, that plan, including any commitments concerning the Union's common priorities, must be taken into account in the design of the macroeconomic adjustment programme.

The amended text underlines in this regard that Regulation (EU) 2024/1263 requires that national medium-term fiscal-structural plans to address the Union's common priorities. According to that Regulation, these common priorities include a fair green and digital transition, including the EU's climate objectives, social and economic resilience, including the European Pillar of Social Rights, energy security, and, where necessary, strengthening defence capabilities.
It is specified that the draft macroeconomic adjustment programme should fully observe Article 152 TFEU and Article 28 of the Charter of Fundamental Rights of the European Union.

The Commission should inform the Chair and Vice-Chairs of the competent committee of the European Parliament of the conclusions drawn from the monitoring of the macroeconomic adjustment programme. That information should be treated as confidential.

Post-programme surveillance should focus on monitoring and assessing the capacity of the Member State concerned to repay the financial assistance received, taking into account the economic, budgetary and financial condition of that Member State. It should also cover the implementation of certain reforms, to the extent that those are not already subject to monitoring under the national medium-term fiscal-structural plan. Finally, post-programme surveillance should identify the need for corrective measures to mitigate risks to the capacity of the Member State concerned to repay the financial assistance received. Post-programme surveillance is without prejudice to the power of other lenders, such as the ESM, the EFSF and other relevant international financial institutions, to carry out tasks under their own legal frameworks.

In order to preserve transparency, accountability and ownership for the decisions taken, the documents and acts to be provided by the Commission to the Council as specified in this Regulation should be made available to the European Parliament without undue delay.

The European Parliament has approved, with amendments, a change to an EU rule that governs how countries in the euro area are monitored when they are in, or at risk of, serious financial trouble. The change aims to bring this rule in line with the EU's reformed economic governance framework from 2024 and with institutional changes since 2013. It also simplifies and clarifies parts of the rule, in line with the Commission's effort to reduce regulatory burdens. The Parliament's vote was 458 in favour, 138 against and 61 abstentions.

When a euro area country asks for financial help from other countries, from the European Financial Stability Mechanism, the European Stability Mechanism or the IMF, it must prepare a draft economic adjustment programme with yearly budget targets. The programme is drawn up with the European Commission, working with the European Central Bank and, where appropriate, the IMF. If the country already has an active national medium-term fiscal and structural plan, that plan, including its commitments on the EU's common priorities, must be taken into account when designing the programme.

The EU's common priorities include a fair green and digital transition, including climate goals, social and economic resilience, including the European Pillar of Social Rights, energy security and, where needed, stronger defence capabilities. The draft programme must fully respect Article 152 of the Treaty on the Functioning of the EU and Article 28 of the Charter of Fundamental Rights of the European Union. The Commission must also inform the chair and vice-chairs of the relevant European Parliament committee about the conclusions it draws from monitoring the programme, and this information is to be treated as confidential.

After a programme ends, monitoring focuses on whether the country can repay the financial assistance it received, given its economic, budgetary and financial situation. It also covers the carrying out of certain reforms, where these are not already monitored under the national plan, and identifies any corrective measures needed to reduce risks to repayment. This monitoring does not limit the powers of other lenders, such as the ESM, the EFSF and other international financial institutions, to act under their own rules.
To keep decisions transparent and accountable, the documents the Commission provides to the Council under this Regulation should also be made available to the European Parliament without undue delay.
